utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: They went to MUP, Gjilan MUP. They know who they spoke to because they knew the person they were supposed to talk to. I don't know that person and I don't know his name because I wasn't present.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you happen to know his rank or is that also a no?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: That's fair enough. And in any event, in your detailed handwritten statement that we've been -- that we received yesterday, that I believe has been marked and utilised today as 4D10, in that handwritten statement of 30 pages, you make no reference to the fact that the three individuals made contact with someone in the police station, the SUP, in Gnjilane. Why was that omitted from your handwritten statement?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, not only on that day, but we had had the opportunity to speak with Gjilan police on many occasions. But I didn't deem it necessary to speak of it because we didn't have any problems. Now I only mentioned those with whom my village had a problem, and those with whom we didn't have problems, I didn't write it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. Fair enough. Now, if we could focus on the three officers of -- the persons you identified as three officers - I'm talking about Palamarevic, and Djilas, and the third individual whose name escapes me at the moment, it was Locki or something - when these individuals advised you that you had to leave your village, did they give you an option of where to go, as to your final destination?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. I said already that we didn't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. And did they, in fact, direct that you were going to end up at the Macedonian border at that point in time?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: We set out in the direction of the Macedonian border at that time. No. We were following the police that was ahead of us. Wherever they were going, we were following after them. That was the order.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, I'd like to direct your attention also to yesterday. We heard about how Mr. Goran Denic, a Serb from your village was ultimately arrested. You had also mentioned an individual named Negovan Denic, and he is also referenced in your handwritten notes. Do you have any knowledge of the fact that Negovan Denic, another Serb from your village, was arrested and detained by the Serbian police, the Serbian MUP, on April the 20th for committing crimes, specifically looting of houses?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I do know the persons involved.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know a gentleman by the name of Ademi Sebastijan [phoen] from the village of Kmetovce?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, there's no person by that name in Kmetofc. There are two families, larger families, in Kmetofc, one by the last name Azizi and the other Latifi. There are no others.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Do you know that between April and May of 1999, the Serbian MUP, the Serbian police, in Gnjilane municipality arrested and detained over 100 persons, including the three individuals I have just named - and these persons were of various ethnicities - for their involvement in looting, burning of homes, thefts, and killings? Do you have knowledge of any of that, sir?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course it's a matter for the police. I don't know anything about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Is that question being put in relation to Prilepnica?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: It includes Prilepnica, Your Honour, yes. The individuals I have named were actually arrested with respect to Prilepnica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From Prilepnica, that is villagers from my village, nobody is arrested.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the two Serbs that we identified before, the Denics, sir. But, in any event, I have just a few more questions for you, and I'd like to first turn to what's been referred to as the OSCE report, which I had it down as Prosecution Exhibit 2288 and which now I guess also has a Defence number. I'll refer to the Prosecution number. And I don't know whether it will assist to put this on the screen, since we only have a copy in English, which the witness does not read. But I'd like to ask you, sir, a couple of questions. Now, the OSCE report that has been given to me has a check box where the interviewer has identified the type of forces that were responsible for the events that you told the interviewer about. And the exhibit that I have, sir, lists the April 6th, 1999 act when your people left the village. It also lists the April 14th incident that we've discussed here today. And for both of those, the OSCE report has the box marked, saying that the police were the parties responsible for committing these acts against you. Did you, in fact, tell the OSCE that the police of Serbia were responsible for these two events?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: From my village?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay. Well, I think that clears up for me whether in fact the OSCE report reflects things --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Can we see that on the report?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Yes, we can, if we put up P2288 --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: It's on the screen. The question is where on the document is the point you're referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: If we can scroll down, I believe it's the second page. Okay. If we could zoom in on the top, right there. If we could see, it references the 6th April 1999 event, and there's a checkmark next to the box labelled "Perpetrators: Police." And then there's blanks for VJ, JNA, blank for KLA, and a checkmark under "Other."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: He hasn't signed this, has he?

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: The testimony from Mr. Hannis -- pardon me, the representations from Mr. Hannis the other day were that he had signed a report but not this particular version of it, I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: That wasn't my representation; that was his answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: All right, sir. Now I've got just a couple more questions for you.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Mr. Shaqiri, we can move away from that document now, and I have just a couple more questions. Now --

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand this.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I apologise, sir. I was just trying to clarify. For me it seemed that the OSCE report did not identify the persons responsible in the same way that you did in your testimony, and you have now cleared that up for me. So I apologise. We were discussing another matter.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you for your clarification.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, my last series of questions deals with your handwritten statement that was submitted to us yesterday and information that I learned based upon that handwritten statement. Now, am I correct that this handwritten -- am I correct that your village, in 1999 - specifically, at least, April of 1999 and for several months prior to then - was housing persons from the Drenica region who did not normally live in Prilepnica?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: And this is a fact that has not been mentioned in any of your other statements or in your testimony the last couple days up until now. Is that accurate?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's accurate.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: I don't think I have any further questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. IVETIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Shaqiri for your time.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, yesterday there were issues over two pieces of translation. I only have an oral indication from the translation service. The first was the question whether the witness had claimed that during his military service he served on the front line. There was a mistranslation, and the accurate translation was that he was in the first echelon, and I think he confirmed that himself yesterday. The other question was whether he had used the expression that his village was burned to the ground. Well, you don't always get the identical translation when you ask two different people to translate something, but that particular phrase was translated, on subsequent checking, as "completely burned", which to the translator is essentially the same. So I hope that clarifies the position with the two outstanding translation issues. Mr. Hannis -- sorry, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I had asked you at the beginning if I might --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yeah.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- have a question or two at the end not covered by my colleagues, and I do have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, carry on.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Hello again, Mr. Shaqiri.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I have some questions about your handwritten statement. Now, this was a statement that you sat down and wrote yourself. Nobody asked you questions. You just had an opportunity to sit down and write your story, as best you could remember it, in your own hand, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, this is Exhibit 4D10, and maybe it can be put up on the screen so that at least, if the Court wishes to, the Court can follow it. I'm starting on page 1.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: You said on page 1 that on the 1st of April - you were talking about a funeral that had gone on - you said, I think referring to the people in your village: "We were watching NATO planes, hoping that soon the event we were waiting for would happen, capitulation of the Serbo-Slav army." My only question about that little statement you wrote there is the part about watching NATO planes. How often were you seeing NATO planes in early April of 1999? Were you seeing them a lot of the time or a little bit of the time? How many were you seeing?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 24th of March, if I am not mistaken, we heard - because we didn't see - the roar of the planes flying. And the fact is that we rejoiced at that because we thought that one day that madness that was happening in Kosova would come to an end, irrespective of who the fault was, one or the other side or both sides. The population rejoiced, and I too rejoiced because we thought that the war would come to an end one day because war brings only bad things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And throughout that early part of April, up through the 14th when you left there, were you hearing at least the NATO planes during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I just said that I heard two explosions which, for the moment, I didn't know where it happened, but later on I found out that it happened in -- at Gjilan barracks. When I passed by, one day I saw it with my own eyes. The planes we -- the planes' noise, roar, we heard now and again, but we couldn't see them with our own eyes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: I'm interested, Mr. Shaqiri, in what you said about "thinking and hoping that one day that the madness that was happening in Kosovo would come to an end." What did you mean by "the madness that was happening in Kosovo"?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, even though in my village nobody had died, in other villages people died every day. I tried to remain within the 6th and 13th and 14th of April. Unfortunately, I did not bring the transcript with me, but I know I bear it. Two innocent women from Zabel, whose family was shelled, and I had to go and attend a burial ceremony on the 29th of March and on the 1st of April. They were not killed from NATO, but there were people in uniforms who, in acts of retaliation against NATO, fired randomly and insulted us. That's why I'm saying that someone has to be held responsible for the crimes committed in Kosova, in other villages, in Zhegra, Lashtice. I went and visited Bodrik village, Mlladov. From the courtyards we pulled out the dead bodies and buried them. Being an imam, I attended several funerals of innocent people, and I know that someone is to blame for that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm going over to page 8 of the English translation of your handwritten statement, and you were talking about the departure from your village on the 6th of April, and you were talking about a man from Drenica. Who was this man from Drenica?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, as a Hoxha of the mosque, I took in 81 refugees from Drenica in my village. They were sick people; one of them was Shefqet Buqiqi, an invalid mistreated and beaten up. There were women, children, elderly. Every reasonable person in the world will assist helpless people. This is what we did. We offered our assistance to them. And I didn't care for the police for doing that. So if there is -- if there is a reason in the world, this should be considered an act of humanity. In the entire commune of Gjilan, the first to open the door to take in people from Drenica were people from Gjilan.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you --

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: This is more than I have in my statement, what I'm saying to you now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Do you remember the question that I asked you just now? Do you remember what I asked you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: The person who was staying with me, I took him in. Shefqet Buqiqi is his name. Him and his five members, they were taken in by me, in my own house.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Here's what you said about that man from Drenica and his family. When you were getting ready to leave you said: "I split the family of the man from Drenica into two groups. I took three persons in my car and the rest were with my brother Ramadan." And then you said this: "I was afraid they would be spotted and then the worst could happen even for me, my family, and also for the guests I had." You were afraid that the man from Drenica would be spotted? Is that what you were afraid of?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until they were in Prilepnica, sheltered in our own houses, I was not afraid. But when they ordered us to leave the village - I'm talking about the 6th of April - because of the looting and the mistreating, of course I was afraid that something would happen to my friend. And I respect friends and guests. And if something wrong happens to him, we would feel bad as hosts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, was this man from Drenica some KLA or a wanted man or somebody that they were looking for? When they came to your village looking for somebody, was this the man they were looking for?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. He was a sick person. He went regularly to see the doctor. He had his young children that went to our school and his wife. First he had his father, who died, and then he was buried in another village in the vicinity of Pristina.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, on page 11 you talk about him again and you say that you were trying to find a vehicle for him to travel in and he finally decided to leave on a truck instead of in a car. So this really was some old man that you were trying to help; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not very old. He was in his 60s, early 60s, I think, but he was sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: At the bottom of page 8 and the beginning of page 9 of the translation, you talk about that moment when you had crossed over into Serbia proper and the police came and told you they had an order for you to go back to your houses and that nothing would happen to you and you should be sure of that. And we talked about that quite a bit yesterday. What you told us yesterday was you were very happy to hear that and you were relieved to hear that; correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In this handwritten statement, you tell us that you said to this policeman: "Sir, don't send us back, according to your will. Don't ruin me and these people here." Now, that doesn't sound like somebody who's pleased to hear that news. You're saying: "Don't send me back. I don't want to go back to my village."

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is wrongly translated, sir. We have nothing against the police. The order was given by the army.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Since you say it's wrongly translated, I need you now to find it in your statement, your handwritten statement. It's probably about halfway through, where you've arrived at the border and the police have told you to go back. And first you say what the policeman said to you and then you say what you said to the policeman. Just read us what is in your statement, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: This is on page 9. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It's 8 and 9, Your Honour, in the English translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: It would be about halfway through the Albanian, I would think. I don't read Albanian, so it would be very difficult for me to find it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It appears to me it may be near the top of page 15 in the Albanian.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I found it, yes. I'm right; the translation is wrong.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Read out the passage in Albanian, please, Mr. Shaqiri.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] "Sir," I told the policeman, "don't turn me back with your own will. Don't put me and my people in a difficult situation," because I wanted to be sure that he had received orders from someone in asking us to do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you know, first thing you told me was you didn't say that, and then you said you were right, you didn't say that, and then you read me almost exactly what I suggested that you said, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, it's not that --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, we can all read the translation here and we all heard what you said, so I don't think we need to go any further into it. I want to ask you about something else. After you turned around, you told us yesterday that you spent the night of the 6th in Dobercan and then returned to your village on the 7th; correct?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: And we had a long discussion yesterday about what happened right after you returned to your village. One of the things we talked about at length was you -- you had said in a statement that every citizen was trying to contact Serbian people that had any kind of influence, to try to keep you from being removed from the village again. And I asked you about that and you said: "Well, I really didn't mean every citizen, some of the citizens." But you gave us, I think, the impression that the people in your village were all working together to try to remain in the village. And then I get a chance to read what you wrote in your own hand, and what you tell us and what you wrote in your own hand was that you went back to the village, and when you arrived on the 7th you were informed that there was going to be a meeting in what you call the oda, the guest-room, of Abdyrrahim Osmani at 1900 hours that day; that you were invited to that meeting, that you were happy that there was going to be such a meeting, but then you were disappointed because it didn't turn out the way you expected. You say: "Somebody accused me of how come I got back in the village and did not lead the people back for they were left on the road." You were being accused of abandoning your people when you stayed in Dobercan and did not escort them back to your village, weren't you? They were saying you'd abandoned them.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: In every people in the world there are uncautious people and this is what some kind of people have said, that this is not a formal statement. Some make jokes as they like.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, you don't say in here that it was jokes, and it gets worse, I think. You told them they should form a headquarters for protection, that you could consult and reach discussions together. And one of them stopped you and said, and this is -- you're quoting what this person said to you: "There's no need for that, Hoxha. Everybody should engage separately and according to his possibilities. Whoever knows somebody can speak on behalf of the village; therefore, there's no need for headquarters or annointing of people." You say that got you embarrassed. So then you said: "Let's appoint some older people." And then somebody said to you: "Hoxha, there's no need for that. They will not come back anymore. There will be no more evictions." And then you talk about many other things being discussed that were not worth mentioning. And that made you -- apparently that got you very angry. Your villagers had lost confidence in you, because then you said this, that you said to them: "You do what you like, inshallah the event that we had will not happen again. If something happens, don't count on Hoxha anymore." So you had a fight there with your villagers, didn't you? You had a big argument? You said yes, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it's a fact we had a big argument.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Well, can he complete reading the last sentence that he just quoted? He stopped in the middle of the sentence.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: "... because I will not face them alone without anyone accompanying me." And that's all the questions I have. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Shaqiri, yesterday Mr. Ackerman was asking you some questions, and at page 2874 of the transcript, line 4, he addressed this issue about why the villagers or contacting Serbs to avoid moving out again. Between the 6th and the 14th of April, were you aware or did you have any news about what was happening in the rest of the province of Kosovo with Kosovo Albanian civilians?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was often informed, I said even earlier, of what occurred in other villages of Anamorava, or upper Morava, in Gjilan. On the 28th of March I went --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Shaqiri, the question is very specific. It relates to the period between the 6th and the 14th of April. It appears to me you're not answering that question. Could you concentrate on the period the 6th to the 14th.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. I didn't understand the question properly. During that period I was focussed on my own village. Of course, I heard things -- about things happening in other places, but at this moment I don't recall that.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And before the 14th of April, were you aware of what had happened to Kosovar Albanians in other villages in Kosovo from the start of the NATO bombing on the 24th of March, 1999?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Partially, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And without giving specific details, generally what had you heard?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: I heard of murders in Vllashtica, Mlladov, Zhegra, and through television I heard of what was going on all over Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Had you heard about other villagers being told to remove -- to remove themselves from their village, as you were on the 6th of April?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before the 14th of April, no, I didn't hear anything.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, at page 9 of the transcript today, line 8, Mr. Bakrac was asking you about your June 2001 statement in which you described being ordered to leave your village. On the 13th and the 14th of April, when you were told that you had to leave, did anyone tell you where you were supposed to go or were you simply told to leave the village?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the 13th and 14th of April, we were told that we would go in the direction of Ferizaj under escort, because I demanded an escort.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And were you told anything more than you were to go in the direction of Ferizaj?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. The destination was Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, I want to ask a couple more questions about your conversation with the three men who came on the 13th and who I believe you testified you spoke to again on the 14th, that is, Djilas, Ljuba Palamarevic, and the third individual. Am I correct that the one who mentioned Belgrade was Djilas?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And Palamarevic is the one who mentioned the headquarters -- the military headquarters in Gjilan?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At page 2281 from yesterday, line 22, when there was a discussion about this, I think at one point you said you could also say it in Serbian, what Djilas had said about that. Can you say it in Serbian? Do you remember what words he used?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Before coming to that, that is, before using that word, we had an argument, a rather fierce argument. It was a driver, Reshat Rrahmani and Djilas. The argument was between the two. When Reshat came to my courtyard, he saw his own director there, and now I can quote. I quoted it once; if you need me, I can quote it again. After that argument, in the presence of all the people that were there, he said: "An order came from Belgrade, from the General Staff." He mentioned Belgrade. "And that you must be evacuated by all means." I said it even before in Serbian.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's correction: Not General Staff but Supreme Staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: The page reference can't be correct if it's from yesterday. It may just be a transposition of --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It may be 2821.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Yes, all right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I hope.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you've answered in part my next question: Who else was present when this was said by Djilas? There was yourself, Djilas. Who else?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. It was Reshat Rrahmani, Demush Bajrami, Rexhep Mehmeti, Ramadan Mehmeti, and I think I mentioned all. I don't know if I have left out someone. And myself of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the next day on the 14th, did you have any further conversation with any of those three about why you had to leave?

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, sir. We were surrounded during the night, and I am repeating it: At 7.30 I left with my car, with my family, and headed the convoy. All the people were out in the streets waiting to leave. They had gathered at the end of the village. Some 100 metres away there is a turning point there from the last houses. This is where the road turns to Gjilan. With an armoured car -- and there was another armoured car a little bit further away. I stopped in front of them and they asked me this: "Have you taken all of them? Do you need any bus or fuel?" I answered that: "I don't need any bus, I don't need any fuel. We are all set. But we only want you to escort us, as we agreed," because I asked them for an escort and they had promised to give me one, because the first time it was very difficult for me to lead my people. And the second time I didn't want to take any risks. And the answer was: "Go on your way. At the well you will find the escort."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the correct citation for the previous comment should be page 2881, line 22 and 23.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Shaqiri, I have no further questions for you. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: With the permission of the chair, I'm going to ask you one or two questions just to understand a few things. My first question is: What was the state of things in the village of which you were the imam between -- and how -- what type of relationship existed between different people of different creed before March 1999? What type of relationships did you have amongst yourselves as different people of different creeds before March 1999? This is my first question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I take pride in what I'm saying, that for generations on end my family has been performing this duty of imam, and we have never had any problems among people from my own population and from other creeds. Even though our village is surrounded by seven Serbian-inhabited villages, we have had good relations, normal relations. They have always passed through our village. That is a civilised people, a well-behaved people, a people that loves God and the mosque. We had a library which had manuscripts in Arabic, in Persian, in Bosnian, in Albanian; it was a true treasury. But on the 14th of April it was destroyed, and Djilas Palamarevic are responsible for that because the library, the mosque, the house of the Hoxha were burned, the house that had served for 100 -- over 150 years. And as I said, I take pride in the civilisation of my people in Perlepnice and its tolerance, which knows no bounds.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Then why this all happened? Do you have your own views about it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know why it happened, but I know that justice and -- justice will prevail. I believe in God.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE CHOWHAN
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: ABDYLHAQIM SHAQIRI [Resumed]
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, Mr. Shaqiri, that completes your evidence. I thank you for coming to the Tribunal to give it. You're now free to leave.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] May I say one sentence, sir? Honourable members of this court, I thank you for your patience. Maybe I was not very accurate in what I said, but I have no experience in being a witness. First of all, I wish you successes, good health, and may justice prevail. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Shaqiri.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Hannis, don't have the next witness brought in just for the moment, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, may I just very quickly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The transcript -- oh, it's already been fixed. The other thing, I want to tender 4D10 and 4D11. I forgot to do that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Well, I don't think you need to because they are incorporated to the extent they've been used in the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just want to make sure the exhibit list shows them as being admitted.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Ackerman -- sorry, Mr. Hannis, the next witness is?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Bajram Bucaliu, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Now, is this the witness we've already dealt with, changing the nature of --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- the presentation --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: -- of the evidence?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: To a 92 bis (D), based on his transcript from the Milosevic case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: And that was authorised after a short discussion in court, was it?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Yes, last week when we thought he might be coming on and --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: All right. Well, it might be best if we had the break just now and then had a complete run of the evidence of the witness. So we'll break now and resume at quarter to 6.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Bucaliu. Would you please make the solemn declaration by reading aloud the document which will now be placed before you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you. Please be seated. Mr. Bucaliu, we have before us a copy of the evidence which you gave when you came here before, so we already have a lot of information about your account of events that relate to this case. The purpose of you being here is to answer specific questions that the counsel involved in the case want to ask, either to clarify things, to supplement them, or to challenge them. It will help all of us greatly if you can listen very carefully to the questions and try to confine your answer to the particular question that is asked of you. The first person to ask you questions will be for the Prosecution. Is that Mr. Hannis on this occasion?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: It is, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Mr. Hannis.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you. Your Honour, this witness will be testifying pursuant to 92 bis (D). His testimony relates to paragraph 72(j), 73, and 75 of the indictment, regarding deportations from Urosevac, Ferizaj municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Sir, for the record, could you state your name and spell your last name, please.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: My name is Bajram Bucaliu.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how do you spell your last name?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: B-u-c-a-l-i-u.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you previously testified in this Tribunal in the trial of Slobodan Milosevic on the 12th and 13th of March, 2002.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: For the record, Your Honour, that is Exhibit P2287, which we would tender at this time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And your prior testimony, as the Judge told you, from four years ago is now going to be part of the evidence in this case. The Judges have it. We won't go through it in minute detail, but I do want to have you explain a few things about it before you're cross-examined by Defence counsel. And to do that I want to ask you a few background questions. First, you're a Kosovo Albanian born in Gjilan, in Kosovo. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes. I am Albanian, born in the Gjilan municipality, Kosova.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]...

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: I have three children. My wife died five months ago.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: My condolences. You, from 1964 to 1999, lived in the village of Fshati i Vjeter, the Serb name which is Staro Selo in that municipality, of Urosevac, Ferizaj?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bucaliu, at page 2059 of the transcript in the Milosevic case, you testified about how on the 2nd of April, 1999, Serb soldiers and tanks came to your village. Where or which direction did they come from when they came to your municipality?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: They came from the direction of the Ferizaj-Gjilan main road to our village. The main road is about 600 metres away from my house. And there were also a lot of tanks that were in the field as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... that were located. Can you tell us geographically where your village is located vis-a-vis Urosevac, Ferizaj?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Vis-a-vis Ferizaj, my village is in the south-east -- to the south-east of Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Approximately how far away?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: From Ferizaj, 3 kilometres.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How big was your village in 1999? Approximately how many houses? How many people lived there?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: In 1999, approximately 100 houses or households, and around 800 inhabitants.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What was the ethnicity of the people who lived in your village?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: It was of mixed ethnicity. Mostly there were Albanians and about 13 families who were of Serb ethnicity. We also had two Roma families.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, on April 2nd, when the soldiers and tanks came, approximately how many soldiers did come, if you saw or noticed?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: I did see them. I cannot say how many soldiers there were, but approximately about 40 to 50. Approximately. I don't know exactly. They were -- they came with tanks, on foot. Maybe there were also soldiers in the tanks; I don't know that as I didn't see them. But approximately up to 40.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How many tanks were there?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Approximately four or five tanks.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what kind of uniforms they were wearing?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, I do recall.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Would you describe them for us, please.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Well, those colours that are usually worn by the Serbian army at that time. The green colour dominated, green and -- and brown mixture.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was it a camouflage pattern?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, a camouflage one.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, did you serve in the military when you were a young man?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes. I completed my military service in 1976/1977.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what did you do in the military? What was your job?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: I served in the aviation branch, in the maintenance of aircraft equipment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you speak and understand the Serbian language?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, I do speak it and understand it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did you learn it, and where?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: We had Serbian neighbours with whom we spent time together, played together, and learned together. Of course, I was taught Serbian also in school, and again during my military service I used it. And I worked with Serbian colleagues, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. You say in your prior testimony, at page 2061, that one of the soldiers that came that day introduced himself to you as a major. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the soldiers told you they were part of the regular army, at page 2062. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: That's correct, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What did you understand by the term "regular army"? What did that mean to you?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: For me, a regular army is an army where I served as well, a regular army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And at that time in Serbia and Kosovo, the regular army was the VJ. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's what it was called.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Mr. Bucaliu, before the 2nd of April, 1999, had there been any significant military or police presence or activity in your village?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: No, not before the 2nd of April, 1999, neither police or military presence.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Were you aware that about nine days before the 2nd of April, that NATO air-strikes had begun in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, we were aware because we saw it with our own eyes and we experienced it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there bombing in your village?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: During the time we were in the village, no, there wasn't.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, in your testimony at page 2062, you indicate that these soldiers asked you for your weapons and that you turned over some hunting rifles; that searches were done and they took your truck. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, everything's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did they tell you why they were taking the weapons?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: No, they didn't tell us why. They just said to us that the people do not need guns. "We are regular army. We will look after you." So this is what they said.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: On the 5th of April, in your testimony at the same page, you say that these regular army forces left your village. In what direction did they go when they left?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: On the 5th of April, around 8.00 a.m., these military forces left the village and went to the Ferizaj-Gjilan main road and set out in the direction of Gjilan.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, before they left, did they do anything or cause any damage in your village?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: As I said, they took my truck, and on that day when they left the village, before they left they torched two houses. These houses were near the main road; that's where they were stationed. So they burned these two houses.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know who those houses belonged to?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: I don't remember the names of the owners at the moment.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you know the ethnicity of the owners?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes. They are Albanians.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recall what time of day they left, approximately?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Around 8.00 in the morning, 8.30. I don't know the exact time, but it was morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We know from your transcript at page 2063, line 2, that later that same day, around 4.00, you describe paramilitary Chetnik forces coming to your village. Where did they come from? Which direction did they come from?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: That is correct, yes. That very same day, although we were happy that these forces left and we thought that that's it, it ended; however, two buses from the other side of the main road Gjilan-Ferizaj, they unloaded about 80 paramilitaries, Chetniks. So they entered from the other side and they slowly began to approach our village and our houses in the neighbourhood where I live.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, these men that you describe as paramilitaries or Chetniks, can you tell us how you distinguished them or differed them from the regular army that had left earlier that day? In what way did they look different?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Well, there is a big difference between them. Amongst them there were people of different ages, ranging between 18 to 60. They had long hair, beards, also cockades. This is what the Serbs call those caps. So they were wearing these cockades. They do differ from the regular army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what was the approximate age range of the soldiers who had been there earlier that you describe as the regular army?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: On the first day, my first encounter with them, it was three soldiers, about 40 years old. Later on we met also other soldiers; some younger and some older.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And was the major one of those three that was about 40 years old?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Are you referring to the major of the regular army that we mentioned earlier or to these Chetnik forces?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No, I was referring to the major of the regular army.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Between 40 and 50, I would say.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, this second group that you described as the Chetnik forces, you've mentioned they had long hair and beards. What about the hair and the facial hair of the forces you described as the regular army that had been there earlier? Did they have long hair and beards as well?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: No, they didn't have long hair or beards. Some had shaved heads; some had shorter hair and regular facial hair. But, no, the army didn't have long hair.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What about the uniforms that the paramilitaries wore? Did they look the same as the regular army?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: The colour was more or less same with the regular army, but as I said, they had other insignia. They had the cockades; they had other things on their uniforms. That's why they differed from the regular army.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you remember anything else about the insignia that they had that might have been different from the regular army?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: I remember that there was this acronym "SCP", which is the Serbian Chetnik Movement. This is what they called it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Where did that acronym appear?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: On the arm.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, at page 2066 of your transcript, you said that: "They informed us who they were" or "who they are." Who did they claim to be, this group of Chetniks that came around 4.00 that afternoon? Do you recall what they told?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember. We spent quite some time with them, about nine days. We had contact with them on daily basis, and of course we heard on a daily basis bits of information from them. They said they were Seselj's men, Seselj's volunteers, who had done the same thing in Bosnia and who had come to Kosova to defend Kosova, to fight in Kosova. We did have many conversations with them, so I really don't know what is more important for you for me to mention. They had taken some young men to dig out trenches and they had told them that "In the end, we will be forced to kill you. This is what we did in Bosnia." And also told them that nobody was supposed to leave the village without their knowledge. "You should be here with us. And if Clinton interferes with his infantry, you will be our shield."

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned in your testimony, I think beginning at page 2095, that you came to know two of the -- at least two of these individuals by names or by first names. Do you recall Mile and Musa?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes. It appeared that these two were the leaders of this group and they had more contacts with them because they were moving up and down the village all the time. And that's why I thought they were the leaders of these soldiers or Chetniks. I don't know what to call them.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You mentioned that you spent about nine days with them. Did you actually see them leave or did you leave first?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: No. We left on 14th of April. They remained in the village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you say "we," who are you referring to?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: I'm referring to the inhabitants of Fshati i Vjeter, of ethnic -- Albanian ethnic origin.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, before you left on April 14th, did anything happen that precipitated your leaving that day? You had been there together with these guys for about nine days. What caused you to leave on the 14th?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Throughout the time while we were in the village, between the 5th and 14th of April respectively, these paramilitaries, Chetniks, they looted us and maltreated us in different ways. We were encircled and we were not permitted to leave the village. And on 13th of April, they killed Emin Zeka and his two sons in the evening. The following day, on the 14th of April, the Hoxha of the village - there is an elderly person in the village who is a Muslim priest - came to my house and told me that Emin and his two sons had been killed the previous night. To tell you the truth, I couldn't believe it because it was hard to imagine that that had actually happened after all the looting and the maltreatment. So around 1300 hours -- I just want to mention that the Hoxha had informed others about this killing as well. So instinctively people began to gather around my house because my house is in the centre of the village. And I saw this mass of people asking themselves: "Why are we waiting here? They have begun to kill us." It is a difficult moment because we didn't know what to do, where to direct the people. So since we thought that they were going to kill us, we thought it would be wise for us to try and escape from the village. There is a valley behind my house and meadows, so all of us - children, women - began to flee. I told my family, my children and my wife, to join them. I had to stay for a while in the village because my mother is paralyzed and she cannot move. And because of her, I had to stay there in the village for some time. So in short, this is how the villagers fled my village.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we see from your prior testimony that you say about 5 or 600 people left the village that day. You stayed with your mom for a while and then joined the group, and your father went back to join your mother, as I understand. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: That is correct. I was forced to leave because my mother was ill. My father wasn't there at the moment. He returned later. After two and a half hours, I left as well. I had to, because my mother begged me to leave. She said: "I am old, and even if they kill me, there's nothing I can do. There's nowhere I can go, but you have to leave." So my mother and my father remained in the village, but later on they fled as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then you tell us in your testimony that the group of 5 or 600 who had fled the village stayed -- went to Ferizaj, stayed there the night, and the next day went to the train station and got on a train that was going toward Macedonia. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. On the 14th, this mass of people, about 500 or 600 people, went to Ferizaj. And on the 15th of April, we were at the railway station in Ferizaj to board the train.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: You tell us in your testimony that that train was -- that had about ten carriages, it was crammed with people, and about 2.500 people got on the train before it set off in the direction of Hani i Elezit, or Djeneral Jankovic, near the Macedonian border. Were you part of that group that got on the train that went toward Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, my family and I were part of this group that boarded the train on the 15th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we read that when you got there that day, you actually did not get to get off the train to go to Macedonia. You waited around for some period of time and then the train was sent back to Ferizaj, Urosevac. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct. At Hani i Elezit railway station we arrived at approximately 9.00. Then we stayed in the train until 12.00 approximately, all of us. And it was really crowded, a heap of people. And since I knew the chief of the station - he was a colleague of mine - I asked him what was going to happen to us. And he informed me that they were contacting the Macedonian authorities, and if the Macedonian authorities accepted us, we would be allowed to leave. And his answer was that the Macedonian authorities for the moment were not accepting us. And in the end, that's what happened. We were told that the Macedonian authorities were not accepting and that train was sent back.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So you went back to Ferizaj, stayed there another night, and the next day you got on the train and made the same trip toward Macedonia; correct?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: That's correct. The next day, the same time in the morning, we got on the train, me and my family and many others, and we continued in the same direction, towards Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Was there any police or soldiers at the train station or on the train on the 15th and/or the 16th of April?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, there were policemen in the train.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What were they doing, if you could tell? Were they just going along for the ride?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: They were not just going along for the ride. I don't know what task they were performing, the security or whatever, but they were in the train wearing their uniforms, their weapons. They were not ordinary policemen; they were policemen on duty.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What kind of uniforms did they have?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: They had a blue uniform.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Is that a solid colour or camouflage?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: To my recollection, a solid colour, those policemen who were on the train.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When you got back to Djeneral Jankovic or Hani i Elezit on the 16th, what happened this time?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: I again asked my colleague, the chief of the station, how it was going to be done on that day, and he told me that they had information that it will move fast. We stayed on the train, all of us, for some 15 minutes. And after these 15 minutes, Vule, the chief of the station, came out and told us that: "Now you're leaving Bajram. Have a pleasant journey." So that train now began to move in the direction of Macedonia. The train left us or stopped at 1.5 kilometres from the border with Macedonia. There we saw soldiers and policemen along a road which is near the railroad. They were boarding a tractor, and they were making a sign for us to get off the train. We were afraid. We didn't dare get off. I was in the first car, and I told the others that they are just giving us a sign to get off, so we did get off the train, all of us. There we stayed for about 15 minutes, and then a military person, since I was the first person near the engine, he said that all of us have to get off the train and to continue walking along the tracks and not to get out of the tracks because that area was mined. So this is what we did. We got off the train and we walked along the tracks to Macedonia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How long did you stay in Macedonia?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: In Macedonia I stayed until the 10th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: When did you eventually return to your home in Kosovo?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: I eventually returned to Kosovo on the 6th of July.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, Mr. Bucaliu, you've talked about this before in your previous testimony, but I would like to go through it again a little bit because I think you're the best person to help me and the rest of us understand this. What work did you do before the war started in 1999? What was your job?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: I worked at a train station in Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And the next exhibit I'm going to deal with, Your Honour, is P1331.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: At the train station what kind of work did you do?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: For a time I was following the trains. I don't know the right word for that. This is how we called it. Then I worked as a cashier. I did various jobs.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how long did you work for the railroad at the train station?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: I worked from 1982 to 1999 at the Ferizaj train station. Before that, I worked in Slovenia.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I would like to hand the witness the original of the document that P1331 is a copy of, and I have passed around some hard copies which are an excerpt from that original because I was trying to save some paper. But because the original is a two-sided document, when it folds out to see the entire two pages, we printed it on this larger paper which covers the time period from the 28th of February until, I believe, the 30th of May, 1999. We have an English translation of the headings of each of the columns in this book, and I would start by asking the witness, Mr. Bucaliu:

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you recognise that book that you have in front of you?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes. That is the original copy of the diary where we kept track of the circulation of trains at that time, log-book.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And where does this come from?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: I found this traffic log-book at the train station in Ferizaj when we returned.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And you brought that original to the Tribunal when you testified in the Milosevic case in 2002?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And when you worked at the train station, did you personally ever make entries into the log?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: No. At that time I wasn't responsible for entering -- for making entries into the log.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: But based on your work there, were you familiar with how this book was used and how the records were kept in it?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Of course I know how it is done because I finished the school in Slovenia precisely for that. This is the main task that one does when working at a railway station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: If you could turn to the page in your book that -- the top line has the date of the 22nd of March, 1999.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And, Your Honours and counsel, this has the ERN number K0218501 and 8502 on your copies.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Have you found that page, Mr. Bucaliu? It has entries for the 22nd and the 23rd of March, 1999, it looks like.

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Am I correct that column number 1 is the date?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: You are correct. The first column indicates the dates.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And under column 2 we see a series of four-digit numbers. What are those four-digit numbers? What do they represent?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: The four-digit numbers represent the numbers of the regular trains used for passenger transport.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And just by looking at the numbers, can you tell us anything about that particular train? For example, the number "7893" at the top, based on that number, what can you tell us, other than it was a passenger train? Can you tell us which direction it's travelling?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes. Based on the number, you can find out the direction of the train. This case, "7893" train went from Fushe Kosove to Hani i Elezit.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what's the Serbian name for Fushe Kosove?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Kosova Polje.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And "7892", which direction would that be travelling?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: That train would be travelling in the opposite direction, respectively, Hani i Elezit-Fushe Kosove.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how are you able to tell that? What is it about the numbers that explains to you which direction the trains are travelling?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: It's a rule that we use odd or even numbers. In this case, the odd number goes in the direction of Hani i Elezit; the even number goes in the opposite direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: So even numbers are going north towards Fushe Kosove. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: How many railroad lines went through Urosevac, Ferizaj? Was there one line or several?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: You mean how many trains travelled a day or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: No. First my question is: How many railroad tracks, actual tracks, go through Urosevac, Ferizaj? Is there only one line or are there several?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: At Ferizaj station there are four lines. But to go from Ferizaj in the direction of Fushe Kosove and Hani i Elezit, there is only one line that goes in that direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Are there passenger trains that go anywhere from Ferizaj, other than to Fushe Kosove or Hani i Elezit, if you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, I understand your question. The direction was the same, but they went to other stations as well. The train that went through Ferizaj might go to Belgrade as well or from Ferizaj to Skopje and even further up to Greece or I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I understand that. But is there -- to go to Belgrade the train would have to pass from Ferizaj through Fushe Kosove before getting to Belgrade; correct?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then to get to Skopje from Ferizaj, you would have to go through Hani i Elezit?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. The next columns, 3, 4, 5, and 6, I see from the English translation, appear to be times. The time under 3 and 4 is the time the train arrived in the station?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And departure time in column 5 and 6?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: What does column 7 show?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Column 7 shows when trains are delayed from the regular time. When we are talking here about the first train, it was 13 minutes late. Instead of 7.33, it came 13 minutes late.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And I see that farther down in that column a few times the letter "R" appears. What does that stand for?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Letter "R" stands for "regular," on time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, typically, in the first few months of 1999 before the NATO bombing started, was there a regularly scheduled number of trains that passed through Ferizaj, Urosevac? Was it always the same number every day or every weekday, if you understand my question?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: I understood your question, and from this log-book you can see that passenger trains were regular trains up till that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And how often would passenger trains pass through Ferizaj going in the direction of Kosovo Polje or Fushe Kosove? How many times a day?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: About ten trains every 24 hours; five in one direction and five in the opposite direction.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: We see that -- it appears that there's an equal number of even-numbered and odd-numbered trains on each day. Is that consistent with your experience while you worked there?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, it is consistent with my experience.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And I have a question for you about this number for the train. How are those numbers assigned to the train? Is there an actual number painted on the train or is that number referred to as the sequence in which the train travels that day, if you know?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: No, it's not painted on the train. But there is a train schedule, and depending on the number we assigned to the train, we determined the category of trains. These with four-digit numbers are local trains that travel to nearby stations, whereas in the case of international trains, they have three-digit numbers. All freight trains have other numbers. So on the basis of the number, we determined the category of the trains.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, if you would turn to the next page.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Your Honours, that would be K0218503 and 8504.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: The first entry on that page refers to the 24th of March, 1999, which, as we know, is the date the NATO bombing started. It appears that some trains did run on that day, but the fifth row down from the top, I see there's some writing across there. Are you able to read that writing? Do you recognise the handwriting? Or can you make it out and tell us what it says?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Are you asking me about this red pencil handwriting? This was done by the person on duty. Here it says that he has checked the tracks at the station and that they are okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. And at the bottom of the page, underneath the last entry for a train on this page, I think it looks like train number 7874, all across the page there is some writing at the bottom of the page. Can you tell us what that says, if you can read it?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, I can read it. Yes, the number. It writes here that: "Electricity was cut off at 2010 and came back at 0540." And then the other person who took over the duty at 7.00 in the evening says that electricity was cut off again at 2000 hours; that the generator worked, and then electricity came back. And then he hands over the duty to the other colleague and so on. It is the same thing. Now, the other entry is about the next day. The electricity was interrupted at 1950, he says. The generator didn't work from 2130. And then there is a column 48, the number of the trains that did not circulate, did not run, but they didn't run during that period -- they were supposed to run but didn't run, that is, from the 24th to the 29th. For five days trains didn't run.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Then on that next page we see the first entry, K0218505 and 8506. At the top it appears to be on the 29th of March the trains were running again. It looks like there were only two trains on the 29th and two on the 30th. And then on the 31st it looks like a more regular schedule. But then I noticed on the 30th, the first train there is listed as 37895 -- 893. That's a five-digit number. What does that tell you about that train? You've explained passenger trains being four-digit numbers. Can you tell us anything about 37893?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, this shows that it is a passenger train and not a regular train, outside the usual hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And is that the reason for the extra digit to indicate that it's a non-regularly scheduled train?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes. This is the reason. We have added the number 3 before 7893, and it shows that it is a non-regularly scheduled train. It's the second part of the regular train by that number, 7893.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And under the 31st of March, I see the first train was 37897. And then 37894, for the time of arrival there just appears to be a diagonal line drawn through there. What does that mean?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Train 37890, not 4. The line shows that it has set off from Ferizaj station. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Farther down under the 31st, the last two trains that travelled that day, I see 37891 and 37890. There's a diagonal arrow drawn under the column for arrival time. What does that tell you about those trains?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: The arrow in this case shows that the trains had passed but not stopped at Ferizaj station.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. So 37891, the odd-numbered train, would have been travelling in the direction of north to south, from Fushe Kosove toward Hani i Elezit, and it passed through Ferizaj without stopping?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, it appears on the next page, which has an entry for the 1st of April at the top, I see another variation on the five-digit numbers where we have 1 -- it looks like -- correct me if I'm wrong, it looks like 14392. What can you tell us about that train?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: The train 392 has the number of the international train. As I told you, the three-digit numbered trains travel outside the country, that is, they are international trains. When this train runs outside the normal hours and wants to pass through this line, we add two digits --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Oh, okay. So this was --

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And what does the "1-4" indicate, then, about this international train 392, that it's not regularly scheduled to travel at that time or through that location?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: That is correct. It was not scheduled to travel at that time. It's running outside the normal hour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Now, it appears that the number of trains travelling each day are increasing during the first part of April, and finally I would like to take you to a couple of dates that you are familiar with. I think if we can go to the 15th of April.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Which on the hard copy Your Honours and counsel have, I believe, is K0218517 and 8518.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Do you find that page, Mr. Bucaliu?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, I found the 15th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And we see at the top of the page, on the 15th of April, train number 7893 - an odd number meaning it would be going toward Macedonia - arrived at 7.43 and left at 8.17. That's about 34 minutes in the station. Is that a long time to stop at Ferizaj, based on your experience and the previous entries in the log-book?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, you are right.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And why was that, if you know?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: This was so. I was present at that time. There were a large number of people who wanted to get on board the train; that was the reason why it had to wait for so long, because there were a large number of people wanting to get on the train.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And immediately below that entry, can you tell us what's written on the line beneath that first entry for 7893?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: This shows only that the person who was on duty handed over the duty at 7.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Okay. Then the second thing and the last thing we see on the 15th is train number 7892, which would have been coming from the Macedonian border, Hani i Elezit to Ferizaj, arrived at 12.38 and didn't depart until 13.32. What do you know about that train?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: This is the train by means of which I returned from Hani i Elezit with my family and with all the other people on the first day. We returned to Ferizaj station. And as you can see, it had to wait long for all the people to get off the train. This is why.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Did you see if that train continued on north toward Fushe Kosove after you got off, almost an hour after it had arrived?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, it continued towards Fushe Kosove without passengers.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Had everyone then gotten off in Ferizaj with you?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, yes. All of us got off at Ferizaj.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: And one more entry for us, please. The 16th of April, we see 7893, which would have been a southbound train, arriving at 7.50 and leaving at 8.10. Is that the train you got on and went to Hani i Elezit on the 16th?

utterances.speaker: BAJRAM BUCALIU
utterances.text: Yes, this is a train I got on on the 16th.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: May I have a moment, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Bucaliu.

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
utterances.text: I have no more questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE BONOMY
utterances.text: What, in all these details of the trains, have we to pay attention to? Just the trains that Mr. Bucaliu was on?

utterances.speaker: MR. HANNIS
